3.text: warm and appears well, but in reality the leather has deteriorated and the

4.text: hair thinned out, so that it offers appreciably less protection from the cold.

5.text: The neck of the inner shirt is often trimmed with a broad strip of dog’s

6.text: or wolf’s fur, as shown on Plate XXIV, Fig. 2. This may be folded back,

7.text: forming a thick and warm collar. The lower edges of both parts of the shirt

8.text: are trimmed with narrow pieces of fur. The inner shirt is a trifle longer, so

9.text: that the garment appears to have a double row of trimming around the bottom.

10.text: This trimming is usually of dog-skin, but in the best shirts wolf, fox, and

11.text: wolverene trimming is used. The last-named is considered the prettiest,

12.text: wolverene-skin being highly prized among the Chukchee and among the

13.text: Eskimo on both shores of Bering Sea.

14.text: The Koryak fur shirt is trimmed below with a broad strip of fur of the

15.text: same material as the body of the shirt, but different in color. This strip is

16.text: commonly bordered with a narrow piece of dark-colored reindeer-skin, and with

17.text: beaver or otter in garments of the well-to-do. The same method of trimming

18.text: fur shirts is adopted by the Russianized Yukaghir and Kamchadal, as well as

19.text: by some of the Chukchee on the Pacific side. On the whole, however, a

20.text: characteristic feature of the Chukchee shirt, distinguishing it from that of the

21.text: Koryak, is the absence of this lower strip.

22.text: The sleeves of the shirts are full at the shoulder, and narrow at the

23.text: wrist. The opening is slightly gathered in, and bordered with a narrow strip

24.text: of fur. If desired, the arms can be drawn out of the sleeves into the bosom

25.text: of the shirt. Indeed, this is a favorite position with the Chukchee when taking

26.text: their ease (see Plate XXVII, Figs. 1, 2). The shirt is so ample, that when the

27.text: arms are drawn in, the man can without difficulty turn in the garment, which

28.text: then looks more like a small tent. When sleeping in the open without an

29.text: overcoat, a Chukchee man makes full use of the shelter of his ample shirt.

30.text: He tightens the belt and then draws in his arms, turns up his fur collar, and

31.text: draws his head inside, and then pulls the front of his thick fur cap up to the

32.text: neck-opening. Fortified in this manner, he can sleep snugly in the most severe

33.text: cold or during a heavy fall of snow. In the morning he will shake off the

34.text: snow just like an animal after sleeping in the open.

35.text: The young people make their upper shirt of thin fawn-skins from the

36.text: first fall slaughtering. These look smoother and neater than the others. The

37.text: inner shirt, of course, has to be made of thicker skins. With the simpler

38.text: clothes the reverse is the case. I have already noted that for colors, dark

39.text: brown, spotted, and pure white are preferred. The young people, too, have

40.text: their shirts short, while those of old men reach sometimes considerably below

41.text: the knees, and are made of the thickest autumn skins. They then look more

42.text: like heavy overcoats than mere shirts.
